1:
The occasion is guessed from the psalm's tone. Henry supposes David wrote it under Saul's persecution, when his enemies dressed him in the skins of wild beasts to bait him; innocency, he observes, is no fence to the name, though it is to the bosom, against the darts of calumny. Clarke reasons from the number of protestations, which suggest a man clearing himself of alleged plots, and reports without adopting a suggestion that this psalm and the two after it are one ode from the captivity. Delitzsch prefers the Absalom conspiracy, and observes that this psalm, bound to the one before it at several points, lacks entirely the self-accusation that there accompanies the attestation of piety. The harshness of the contrast with these enemies leaves no room for such a lament.

What the appeal asks for divides them. Ellicott renders it do me justice, vindicate me. Calvin points out that the verb denotes the act of a judge and of an advocate alike, and prefers the second as agreeing with the psalm's scope; when God leaves us to our enemies he seems to neglect our cause, but when he restrains them our defence is shown to be his care. Henry keeps the judicial sense: Saul was himself supreme judge in Israel, so in a controversy with him David could appeal to no other than God. Gill draws the distinction that decides the psalm: this is not the justification of his person, which he knew was not by his own righteousness, but of his cause before men. Clarke makes the denial specific: he never plotted against any man's life or property, nor coveted Saul's crown. Spurgeon warns against borrowing the prayer carelessly. He had need have a clear case who dares carry his suit into the King's Bench of heaven; as to the whole of a man's walk the appeal should never be made except as he is justified in Christ. Where conscience approves, though, the comfort is great — when the little bird in one's bosom sings a merry song it is no matter if a thousand owls hoot from without.

Henry states the limit as doctrine: David cannot justify himself against the charge of sin, but he can against the charge of hypocrisy, as Job owns he has sinned and yet holds fast his integrity. Augustine builds the qualification into the sentence: he pleads some desert of innocence only after the mercy God first showed him, trusting not in himself but in the Lord. On the request to be tried he is more explicit — let the proving make me known not to thee, from whom nothing is hid, but to myself and to men, and let the burning of the reins be a remedial purgation applied to my thoughts. He assigns the psalm neither to David alone nor to Christ, but to the Church now perfectly established in him. Clarke says it plainly, wishing every motive of his heart dissected and exposed to God's view; Gill supplies the figure of gold tried by the touchstone. Ellicott adds that the verb translated try should on the right reading be purify, the Greek reading tried by fire.

The ground of the plea is the clause about lovingkindness, and here they converge. Delitzsch defines the pair: the first is divine love condescending to sinners in unmerited kindness, the second the truth with which God adheres to that love and to his promise — the one the model of the psalmist's life, the other the boundary of his walk. Ellicott puts it in a sentence: God's favour before him as encouragement, God's truth as the rule of his life. Wesley makes it the reason he dares appeal at all: thou knowest I have a deep sense of thy lovingkindness, which led me to love and obey thee. Gill traces it through the choice of him in Christ to a love from everlasting.
4:
The company avoided is characterised differently by each reader. Delitzsch takes the word behind vain persons in a stronger sense than English carries: the chaotic void of alienation from God, untruth whitewashed over with the lie of dissimulation. The second class he calls the veiled, men who keep their mischievous designs secret and mask them by hypocrisy. Clarke reads the two classes politically: men of lies and backbiters, then the hidden ones, the secret plotters in the state. Ellicott is content with hypocrites. Gill spreads a catalogue — men addicted to the world's vanities, unruly talkers, and men guilty of idolatry. On the congregation of evildoers Ellicott notes that the word carries the idea of violence, from a root meaning to break in pieces; Clarke hears politics, crowds of discontented men who under pretence of rectifying the state strove to subvert it. Gill adds that what the psalmist hated was their works, not their persons.

Spurgeon turns the avoidance into evidence. A man is known by his company, and having kept apart from the wicked tells in his favour should his character be impugned — he who was never in the parish is not likely to have stolen the corn, and he who never went to sea did not scuttle the ship. We must see and trade with men of the world, he concedes, but must not take our rest in their empty society; and since hypocritical piety is double iniquity, acquaintance with pretenders should cease.

Whether the washing and the circling of the altar are things done or things said divides them. Delitzsch says the motive of the petition is love for a sanctuary from which the psalmist is now far removed through no fault of his own, and that what is elsewhere a symbolic act appears here only as a figure of innocence. Ellicott traces the same movement historically, the washing first a symbolic action and afterwards a figure of speech. Henry takes it as real preparation, habitual in keeping the conscience clean and actual in alluding to the priests' washing as they went in to minister — for though David was no priest he would look to the substance of what they were enjoined in shadow. He adds that hypocrites attend the ordinances too, as the proud Pharisee went up to the temple with the penitent publican, so sincerity is shown by manner and not attendance. Gill hears the same priestly allusion and adds the lifting up of holy hands in prayer; Wesley reduces it to an impossibility — he could not approach the altar with any comfort if conscious of the crimes alleged.

Spurgeon is careful about how much is claimed: not perfect innocence but innocence of the crimes slanderously charged — though there is a sense in which a man may be washed in absolute innocence, since the atoning blood makes clean every whit. Priests unto God must be personally cleansed, the brazen laver being as needful as the golden altar. Clarke supplies the practice: washing the hands sometimes declared innocence of a base transaction, as when the governor did it at Christ's trial; and walking round a superior or a temple is a mark of respect elsewhere. Ellicott is sceptical about the circling: there is no other reference in Jewish literature to pacing round the altar, though the Talmud implies that at one feast people marched round it with palms. From the comparison of the washing with the command about the laver he draws a conclusion the others never reach: the psalm is Levitical in authorship, or at least in character. The purpose is named at the end: what was to be offered on the altar so compassed, Gill observes, was not a slain beast but the sacrifice of praise. Clarke makes it consistency — he had professed faith, and his practice gave no lie to it.
8:
The love of the sanctuary is read closely. Clarke would translate the verse as the habitation of thy house and the place of the tabernacle of thy glory, the first being the holy of holies and the second the mercy seat — and he derives from the word for dwelling the familiar name for that manifested presence. The psalmist attended these duties, he adds, not because they were incumbent on him but because he loved the place where the honour dwelt. Gill notes that the temple was not yet built, so the tabernacle is meant.

The petition that follows is heard three ways. Ellicott takes it as a prayer to be spared while doom falls on the evildoers, the Greek and Latin reading destroy not. Clarke and Wesley hear it of the final lot: as I never loved their company, let not my eternal portion be cast with theirs. Gill allows both, that he might not be brought into such company or destroyed with them, and observes that death is regularly described as a gathering to one's people. Spurgeon gives the figure its most concrete form — when, like fruit, I must be gathered, put me not in the same basket with the best of sinners, much less the worst — and grounds the request in the earlier verses: a man who kept clear of the profane may fairly ask not to be thrust into their company at the last. On the hands full of mischief, Gill distinguishes mischief contrived from mischief committed; Clarke identifies the men as officials who took bribes to pervert judgment.

The turn to the psalmist's own case draws Spurgeon's sharpest writing and his most careful qualification at once. Here is the lover of godliness entering his protest against unrighteous gain, ready to stand alone, swimming like a live fish against the stream. But he is no boaster, since in the same breath he cries for redemption and pleads for mercy: our integrity is neither absolute nor inherent but a work of grace marred by infirmity, so that saints must still bow as sinners. Clarke reads the resolve as a rule for public life, all public affairs to be handled with strict attention to truth and justice. Gill turns the walking forward, taking it as faith that after he is gathered by death he shall walk in uprightness and perfection.

The last verse is where they disagree about what has already happened. Delitzsch calls it the epilogue, prayer changing into rejoicing certain of its answer: hitherto shut in as though in trackless gorges, the psalmist now feels himself on a plain commanding a wide range of vision, and blends his praise with the congregation's song. Spurgeon hears the same modulation — the song began in the minor and has reached the major key, and saints often sing themselves into happiness — and identifies the even place as the covenant faithfulness of God. Wesley agrees the ground is already sure, under the protection of God's promise. Ellicott alone will not have it: it seems to him more in accordance with the drift of the poem to read the verse as a condition rather than a report — when I stand in an even place, when I am rescued from the difficulties that beset me, then I will praise Jehovah in the congregation. Clarke, who takes the standing as accomplished, lists what it rests on: to abhor evil and cleave to good, to avoid the wicked, to frequent the ordinances, and to depend for salvation on mercy alone. Gill locates it on Christ as the sure foundation. Spurgeon closes the psalm as it closes itself, in company: let us not forsake the assembling of ourselves together, since each saint is a witness to divine faithfulness — and as for the slanderers, let them howl outside the door while the children sing within.
